Within the section on cultivating great wisdom, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the obstacles;
second, clarifying their abandonment.
"To attain this equality and have no other illness except the illness of emptiness" refers to the obstacles.
Bodhisattvas prior to the stages attain [this] within the provisional teachings regarding all phenomena.
Because those conditions are in harmony, they possess the nature of non-existence and are therefore empty.
One does not perceive any distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa;
thus, it is said that one has attained this equality.
It is solely because one relies on emptiness that one no longer clings to existence.
Since the perception of illness has been forever forgotten, it is said that there is no further illness.
This teaching of emptiness is expounded in order to dismantle the perception of illness.
Although the illness has been eliminated, one still clings to emptiness and does not relinquish it.
Because emptiness is not relinquished, emptiness itself returns to become an illness.
Therefore, it is said that there is only the illness of emptiness.
Question: Is it only the mind that takes emptiness as its object that is the affliction,
or is the empty object itself also an affliction?
Answer: There are two different explanations.
If one follows the interpretation of the masters of the Southern Route:
An empty mind and an empty environment are both illnesses.
The reason for this is that the environment is a transformation of the mind.
Objects do not exist apart from the mind.
Since the mind is itself an illness,
objects are likewise an illness.
If, at the time of abandonment, one abandons only the mind,
then objects will naturally not arise.
This is according to the explanation of the masters of the Northern Path.
The mind that takes emptiness as its object is the sickness;
the objective realm of emptiness is not the sickness.
The reason for this is as follows:
The true Dharma of the empty realm— how could it be a sickness?
It is because the mind conditions the realm and gives rise to perverse attachment that the mind is the sickness.
Therefore, at the time of abandonment, one abandons only the mind and not its object;
although there are these two schools of thought.
Now, relying on the previous meaning,
the preceding section has clarified the raising of obstacles;
this is stated according to the underlying principle.
This dedication ultimately aims to enter the first stage (*bhūmi*), yet there are many obstacles.

The text here is abbreviated and thus not exhaustive.
Now, as for the "sickness of emptiness," it refers to the untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) of the mind that takes emptiness as its object.
"Emptiness and illness are both empty" clarifies that by overturning obstacles, one manifests severance;
this was originally intended to explain emptiness.
Because there was illness for him;
once the illness has been dispelled,
emptiness must also be eliminated.
Therefore, the treatise says:
"The Great Sage taught the Dharma of emptiness in order to bring about detachment from all views."
If a person is attached to emptiness,
they cannot be transformed by any Buddha; therefore,
it is said that "the sickness of emptiness is also empty."
The foregoing clarifies the completion of the cultivation of great wisdom (*mahājñāna*).
That is to say, from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) up to the diamond-like stage (*vajropama-bhūmi*), this constitutes the entire locus of cultivating great wisdom.
However, because the ritual procedure is now being performed at a difficult location, we shall for the time being further explain the mind of the first stage.
The first section, on the cultivation of wisdom, is hereby concluded.

A question is asked:
Question: Among all practices, why cultivate only the two practices of wisdom and compassion?
Answer: Because the two practices of wisdom and compassion encompass all practices completely.
Therefore, it is explained specifically:
when one speaks of cultivating wisdom, it is self-discipline;
when one speaks of cultivating compassion, it is disciplining others.
In terms of practicing non-abiding in saṃsāra, one differs from ordinary worldlings;
in terms of practicing compassion while not abiding in nirvāṇa, one differs from śrāvakas;
and in terms of practicing wisdom, one attains the name of a bodhisattva.
Regarding the cultivation of compassion, one attains the title of Mahāsattva;
regarding the cultivation of wisdom, it relies on the ninefold mental state of wearying detachment to seek the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*).
Regarding the cultivation of compassion, it is accomplished by relying on the mind of profound mindfulness for sentient beings.

Regarding the cultivation of wisdom, it is accomplished by relying on the ethical discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) and the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*). Regarding the cultivation of compassion, it is accomplished by relying on the ethical discipline of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
As for the accomplishment of the cultivation of wisdom, it results in the perfection of the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) together with the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
Regarding the cultivation of compassion, it immediately constitutes the virtue of grace;
regarding the cultivation of wisdom, one attains the Dharmakāya and the Sambhogakāya;
regarding the cultivation of compassion, one attains the Nirmāṇakāya.
Therefore, wisdom and compassion universally encompass all practices.
Regarding the cultivation of compassion herein,
the text is again divided into two parts.
The first clarifies the cultivation of minor compassion (*karuṇā*),
which pertains to the stage prior to the [ten] grounds (*bhūmi*).
The second, beginning with "That sick bodhisattva should reflect that my illness is neither real nor existent," clarifies the cultivation of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
This refers to the "stages" (bhūmi).
Regarding the aforementioned minor compassion (*karuṇā*), first its underlying intent is discussed, and subsequently its textual meaning is explained.
As for discussing its intent:
Bodhisattvas prior to the stages who have come directly cultivate minor compassion (*mṛdu-karuṇā*).
The essential nature and characteristics of this minor compassion consist of the object-condition of sentient beings (*sattvālambana*) and the object-condition of phenomena (*dharmālambana*).
Because this compassion takes those beings to be converted as its object, it is called the object-condition of sentient beings.
The method of using compassion as the object for transforming sentient beings is called "conditioned by phenomena" (dharmālambana).
However, when one wishes to teach and transform sentient beings who have committed offenses,
it is necessary to undergo the bodies of the six realms of existence— just like those beings themselves— in order to be able to gather and transform them.

If it is because the great spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*) of the various Bodhisattvas on the stages are so vast that they are able to manifest transformations into the bodies of the six realms of existence to gather and transform sentient beings accordingly,
whereas the Bodhisattvas prior to the stages possess small spiritual powers and thus cannot manifest such bodies.
If one does not transform and teach them, one further violates the bodhisattva precepts.
However, a bodhisattva must now employ those very delusions, karma, and afflictions to undergo bodies within the six realms of existence.
A question is asked:
Question: Where do the bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi) have afflictions? Answer:

As for the afflictions of the four abidings (catvāraḥ nivāsāḥ), based on the supernormal powers (ṛddhi-bala) of those bodhisattvas prior to the stages, they are all able to sever and exhaust them completely.
Because one intends to moisten karma with these delusions in order to undergo rebirth, there is the distinction between their severance and non-severance.
As for the *ekadeśasthāna-bhūmi* (the stage of abiding in a single portion),
Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) suffer from them all and have completely severed them, leaving nothing remaining to be discarded.
The three cravings that abide in their foundational state remain and are not severed;
yet the three feelings that manifest are both severed and no longer retained.
Because these manifest states are severed, one differs from those ordinary worldlings.
Because they abide in the stage of non-retrogression, they differ from the śrāvakas.

Taking these three types of sensation as the basis for the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of afflictions, they moisten the karma of the six realms of existence that has existed since beginningless time, further augmenting it with the power of compassionate vows.
For the sake of this principle, and for the sake of that principle, they are able to receive birth within the teachings of the six destinies to perform their work of transformation;
yet, these bodhisattvas receive such births due to actual afflictions and karma.
Therefore, even when entering hell, they experience only light suffering;
because they undergo this suffering, they quickly develop weary detachment,
yet by the power of their compassionate vows, they return to enter therein once more.
Such is the manifestation of compassion for bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
Although the text divides this into two distinct parts,
the first correctly elucidates the cultivation of compassion.
The second section, beginning with "Mañjuśrī," clarifies the concluding praise that reveals its excellence.
Within the first section on the actual cultivation of compassion, there are five sequential stages of development.
"Subsequently, there is the sick bodhisattva who, by means of non-appropriation...
This first clarifies the self-appropriation [of the teaching].
"The sick bodhisattva" refers to a bodhisattva from the second moment of the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-vijñapti*) up to the final mind of the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
These bodhisattvas calculate that their capacities enable them to sever the bodies of sentient existence— the retributive fruits of the six realms.
Therefore, it is said that while they "receive no [retribution]," they nevertheless undergo all sensations.
This is the second [point], clarifying that he manifests for the sake of sentient beings.
Out of compassion, he desires to transform living beings;
therefore, he manifests by taking on bodies within the six realms of existence.
Therefore, it is said that while experiencing various sensations,
one does not extinguish those sensations to attain realization until the Buddha-dharma is fully perfected.
This is the third point clarifying that sensation does not cease.
As long as one has not yet attained the Buddha-dharmas of the first bhūmi and above,
one will never extinguish the causes for receiving a body within these three realms of existence by realizing cessation through the path of the śrāvaka.
Even if one’s own body experiences suffering, one should contemplate sentient beings in the evil destinies and give rise to great compassion.
This is the fourth [point], clarifying compassion based on birth [in the realms].

It clarifies that although bodhisattvas undergo slight suffering within the hells, they give rise to great compassion because they keep sentient beings in mind, rather than giving rise to weariness or detachment.
Regarding the term "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*):
in reality, it is a case where "small compassion" (*karuṇā*) is designated by the general name "great.
As for the statement, "Since I have been tamed, I shall likewise tame all sentient beings":
This is the fifth section, clarifying how transformation arises based on compassion (*karuṇā*).
Within this text, there are three distinct parts in sequence;
this is the first, clarifying the mind that initiates transformation.
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"Because I cultivate wisdom, I have benefited myself and brought myself under control; now I must further cultivate compassion and likewise bring all sentient beings under control.
I shall merely eliminate their illness without eliminating the phenomena."
This is the second clear understanding of what is appropriate for transformation:
the patient is the mental factor and the disease is the object.
The object possesses delusion.
When one examines these delusive objects, they arise from the mind;
by simply severing the mental state, the objects will naturally cease to arise. Therefore, one does not eliminate the phenomena themselves.
As for its true state, it is fundamentally indestructible;
how, then, could one speak of its removal?
Therefore, the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* says:
Regarding the three natures, how many should be known and how many should not be known?
The answer is: all of them should be known.
"How many should be abandoned and how many should not be abandoned? He replied:
"Two natures are not to be abandoned."
The one nature can be severed.
Because the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is fundamentally non-existent, it cannot be severed.
Because the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is truly existent, it cannot be severed.
Because the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) exists through the combination of conditions, it can be severed.
A question is asked:
"The existence of the dependent nature through the combination of conditions may be granted."
By contemplating this, one attains the non-arising of conceptual discrimination.
One should not contemplate that which is invariably non-existent in order to attain signlessness.
He replied:
The observation of phenomena is distinct from the abandonment of phenomena;
the meaning is as explained in detail elsewhere.
This refers to instructing others in order to sever the root of their afflictions.
This is the third [section], clarifying the characteristics of his transformation.
From here on, he proceeds with a question:
"What is called the root of illness? It is said to be having攀緣 (pān-yuán, objective clinging). This is the answer.
Regarding "the root of illness is clinging":
when each moment of mind grasps at external objects, this is called clinging.
From the presence of such clinging, it becomes the root of illness.
Since the mere presence of a mind is capable of giving rise to illness, it is called the "root.
Below, he asks about the locus of攀緣 (pān-yuán, object-conditioning): what is it that conditions?
"In what location does this affliction of the disease of clinging arise?
The answer is: "It is called the three realms.
Within the three realms, there is clinging.
To be able to give rise to [insight] from below, one asks how to sever the攀緣 (pān-yuan, object-conditioning/grasping) in order to take up the Dharma.
"How does one sever object-conditioning? is the question.
"By means of non-apprehension; if there is non-apprehension, then there is no object-conditioning" is the answer.
That which is non-apprehensible is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
He instructs them to practice the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*) and non-arising (*anutpāda*).
To contemplate that the essence of the mind is empty is called "non-apprehension."
Since the mind has nothing to grasp,
there is no objective support for clinging; since there is no clinging, [there is no further arising].
What is the root of illness?
What is meant by "that which is unobtainable"?
Regarding that which is obtained, one should further inquire about the contemplation of the unobtainable.
Based on what is it established? The answer below states:
namely, that the two views also possess both the action (karma) and the agent (kartṛ).
This is because the meaning of being "separate from the two views" is essentially identical [to the previous case].
This clarifies the answer.
Not giving rise to two views is called "non-attainment.
What are these two views? This is the further question regarding the characteristics of the two views.
He replied:
"The statement that 'internal views and external views are non-existent'— here,
'internal' refers to the sense faculties."
The "external" refers to sensory objects (*dharmas*).
When the mind takes these two as its objects, it is called "the two views.
Furthermore, the "internal" refers to *nirvāṇa*.
The external refers to birth and death.
Because these two serve as conditions, they are called the "two views.
[The Buddha] teaches all sentient beings to contemplate the signlessness of phenomena and to contemplate that signs are unarisen.
Therefore, it is called "non-attainment.
The preceding section concludes the cultivation of minor compassion;
from here on, the text provides a summary and praise to manifest its excellence.
First there is the formal formulation, followed by the eulogy.
"Mañjuśrī, this is how a sick bodhisattva disciplines his mind" clarifies the formulation.
From here below begins the eulogy, which praises the practice and reveals its excellence.
First, the explanation is established through the use of analogies;
subsequently, these analogies are applied to the severing of the suffering of old age, sickness, and death.
This is the bodhi of the Bodhisattva.
To sever the suffering of old age, illness, and death for sentient beings is the path of a bodhisattva;
this clearly demonstrates its benefit.
If it were not so, that which one has cultivated and refined would be without wisdom or utility.
If one does not act in this way by simultaneously severing [the afflictions of] sentient beings,
then the deeds performed by the bodhisattva will lack the benefit of bestowing grace upon the multitude;
moreover, it will manifest as being detrimental.
The following provides an analogy:
Only one who has conquered his enemies can truly be called a hero;
likewise, a person who first eliminates his own [faults] is then able to subdue the enemy forces of others.
This is called "Victory over the Enemy," which is to say, being courageous.
From this point downward, those who simultaneously eliminate old age, sickness, and death are what is meant by a Bodhisattva.
In this way, a bodhisattva eliminates old age and death for themselves while simultaneously [eliminating them] for others; only when one does so is one entitled to the designation "bodhisattva.
The above has clarified the cultivation of minor compassion (*karuṇā*).
From here below, the cultivation of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is elucidated.
Great compassion is precisely objectless compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*).

the second, beginning with "When performing this contemplation," clarifies the cultivation of compassion based on that contemplation.
The prior citation of non-conceptual contemplation is none other than the aforementioned Great Wisdom.
That sick bodhisattva should form this thought: "Just as my own illness is not truly existent, so too the illnesses of all sentient beings are neither true nor existent.
A sick bodhisattva is one who has attained the first bhūmi and above.
Because there is attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), they are collectively termed "those who are ill.
To incite the mind toward contemplation, it is said: "One should form this thought.

Just as this illness of mine is neither real nor an existent dharma,
so too the grasping at afflictions is called "this illness.
That which is not real nonetheless exists.
That which is non-existent is empty.
Contemplating this cause of illness,
it is neither empty nor existent.

it does not exist.

What is its purpose? Answer:
To cultivate great compassion, one must necessarily attain this non-conceptual [wisdom];
without this contemplation, the mind of compassion takes conditioned existence as its object and may give rise to deep attachment.
By means of this contemplation, great compassion constantly transforms sentient beings according to their existence, yet remains free from deep attachment.

this is followed by a brief inquiry and explanation.
When performing this contemplation, if one gives rise to great compassion based on affection or views toward sentient beings, one should immediately abandon it.
This clearly explains the relinquishing of limited compassion.
Once one has cultivated the aforementioned True Contemplation (*bhūta-darśana*),
at the moment when one realizes that the illnesses of both oneself and others are neither real nor existent, [limited compassion is abandoned].
If there were further sentient beings whom one loved and desired to deliver,
such great compassion would indeed have to be relinquished.
From here below, the text poses questions and provides explanations.
Why is this? It is because of subtle inquiry.
Seeing sentient beings whom one loves and desires to deliver—this is a virtuous practice.
Why is it that one should immediately abandon [them]?

To explain the meaning of this:
For those prior to that stage, there are two faults regarding their attachment, views, and minor compassion;
therefore, these must be abandoned.

If there were no great compassion,
one would be unable to constantly transform those sentient beings and enable them to leave their bonds behind;

In this passage, two faults are set forth regarding that limited compassion (*parīttakaruṇā*).
The first sentence clarifies the fault that such limited compassion is unable to bring about liberation from bondage;
the second sentence reveals the deficiency that it is unable to effect constant transformation.
Regarding the Bodhisattva’s severing of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*) and the arising of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*):
this clarifies that minor compassion cannot bring about liberation from bondage.
A "Bodhisattva" here refers to one from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward.
In this context, by severing adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*), one attains objectless great compassion (*anālambana-mahākaruṇā*).
However, compassion based on attachment and views is subsumed under the afflictions of grasping;
because it constitutes a bondage, it must be abandoned.
The "adventitious dust" refers to the nine kinds of adventitious latent tendencies (*anuśaya*): the latent tendency of greed,
the latent tendency of hatred, and the latent tendency of delusion.
1. The four extremely heavy states of mind consisting of greed and hatred; 2.
Abandonment [of these]; 3. Ignorance; 4.
The path of seeing (darśanamārga).
The seven paths of cultivation,
the eight afflictions of the impure stages—
these nine types arise subsequent to the purified mind and depend upon the other-dependent nature.
For this reason, they are called "adventitious dust.
Because they defile what is pure, they are termed "dust" (*rajas*).
Among these nine [afflictions], six are afflictions belonging to the internal realm.
Three of these are afflictions external to the [three] realms.
Speaking in terms of principle,
it is said that only the first five exhaustively encompass the categories of afflictions.
It is simply that the latter four [categories] encompass the exhaustion of the classes of afflictions;
it is simply that the latter four encompass the completion of the classes of afflictions.
However, nine types are taught in order to distinguish the essential nature of the afflictions and the differences in the stages of their abandonment.
Among the nine types, the great compassion of attachment and views pertains to all four categories;
that is, it includes latent tendencies of greed, latent tendencies of hatred, latent tendencies of delusion, and those abandoned through the path of cultivation.
For this reason, the great compassion of attachment and views cannot be free from bondage.
From here below, it is clarified that those whose great compassion is characterized by craving and views cannot transform others constantly.
Those whose compassion is based on craving and views harbor weariness toward saṃsāra;
such compassion, being rooted in craving and views, employs the very delusions, karma, and bodies of craving to perform its teaching and transformation.
Because one undergoes birth due to delusion and karma, the body experiences light suffering, which gives rise to weariness and aversion.
Because weariness and aversion arise, one is unable to constantly transform [beings] within the cycle of birth and death.
For this reason, it is necessary to relinquish [the body].
The foregoing concludes the relinquishing of minor compassion (*karuṇā*).
From here below, the cultivation of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is correctly elucidated.
Within the section on great compassion, the text proceeds as follows.
The first two lines clarify the benefit of constant transformation despite the absence of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
From the second line onwards, they clarify the benefit of [attaining] *...* despite the absence of great compassion.
If one can remain free from these two forms of weariness, [one achieves this].
This clarifies that if one can abandon this compassion born of attachment and views,
one will attain the objectless great compassion (*anālambana-mahākaruṇā*) of that stage;
manifesting transformed bodies, one follows the six *pāramitās* to teach and transform sentient beings.
Although they dwell within the three miserable realms, they are free from painful contact;
they are always able to gather and transform sentient beings without weariness or fatigue.
From this point downward, the second section clarifies that even without great compassion, there is the benefit of liberation from bondage.
The sequence of the text consists of five sections:

The third section cites scriptural authority to establish the proof;

Since there is neither expectation nor opposition, the true mind is quiescent;
therefore, it is called "inconceivable."
If one relies on the delusory to seek the real,
the real exists outside of the delusory;
yet the true reality beyond the delusory is inaccessible to the conditions of emotional attachment.
It is named "Inconceivable" (acintya), for verbal expression cannot reach it; it is beyond deliberation.
Other meanings are explained extensively in the commentary (*śāstra*).
The practice cultivated was clarified in the "Chapter on the Previous Inquiry into Illness" within the section on conduct free from faults;
the realization accomplished is revealed in the "Chapter on the Inconceivable" within the section on conduct free from faults.
Therefore, this chapter follows.
In this chapter, there is a section where Śāriputra reflects upon his seat and Vimalakīrti manifests inconceivable virtues.
Second, there is a section where Śāriputra speaks, and following that, he praises Vimalakīrti, who then orally proclaims inconceivable matters.
The third section is when Mahākāśyapa, lamenting the inconceivable person whose eloquence Vimalakīrti has displayed,
proceeds to the first part of the text, which further clarifies the recollection of the seat.
Second, Vimalakīrti’s instruction and reprimand;
third, his taking of the seat.
At that time, Śāriputra [saw] the couches and seats and had this thought: "Where shall these bodhisattvas and great disciples sit? Having thus completed his first reflection, he [looked about].
The mindfulness of the seat arises because the previous chamber is empty;
if the chamber were not empty, it would not arise.
Reflecting on this, he thought there was no way for him to reach the wondrous seat of the King of Lamps.
It is asked:
For what reason did Śāriputra repeatedly give rise to such thoughts?
The answer is:
This sutra refines the śrāvakas, causing them to weary of the Lesser Vehicle and rejoice in the Greater Vehicle.
Among the śrāvakas, Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom.
His mindfulness was immediately rebuked;
it was known that he was inferior to the śrāvakas,
and even his wisdom was censured and disparaged.
He causes those others to feel self-disparagement for their own narrowness and inferiority, so that they may joyfully seek the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, although Śunetra was foremost in intelligence,
he did not take it to heart.
Mindfulness necessarily manifests the Dharma.
For this purpose, one repeatedly gives rise to mindfulness.
From here below, the second section clarifying the scriptural text contains two parts.
The first [section] clarifies the words of formal admonition and reprimand.
The second, from "Having spoken thus" onwards, clarifies the benefits of such formal admonition and reprimand.
The passage beginning with "Now, those who seek the Dharma" clarifies the instruction.
Regarding the teaching on the refutation and resolution, [the section] from "is thus" onwards is the summary.
Within the teaching on the correct instruction (*samyag-śāsana*), there are further two parts.
The first is the relinquishing of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the second point, "Why is this so? and below, it clarifies that those possessing signs (*nimitta*) are not true [reality]. Within this section, there are further two parts:
first, the clarification of abandoning defiled signs.
Next, [the passage] beginning with "only the śarīra... clarifies the characteristics of relinquishing purity.
As for its intended meaning:
because the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) cannot be attained [through grasping], those who seek the Dharma must not seek it within that which is defiled or pure.
Therefore, [the meaning of] "understanding" cannot be accommodated by the path of words.
Regarding the second point, which clarifies that there are characteristics, it is not a matter of seeking the Dharma; rather, it is a formal inquiry.

As for why one seeks the Dharma by equally relinquishing the marks of defilement and purity, there are ten phrases below. [The commentary] explains that these ten phrases of the sūtra text are subsumed into five pairs.
The first section consists of two sentences,
one pair clarifying that those who perceive signs of purity are not truly seeking the Dharma.
The subsequent section consists of eight sentences in four pairs, clarifying that those who perceive signs of defilement are not truly seeking the Dharma.
Within the preceding pair concerning the pure characteristics,
the first phrase clarifies that those who give rise to mental states toward phenomena and grasp at them as having sentient beings are not seeking the Dharma;
the second phrase clarifies that those who perceive characteristics within phenomena and possess a mind of attachment are not truly seeking the Dharma.
The preceding phrase refers to being free from the pure mind;
the subsequent phrase refers to being free from signs.
The statement that "dharmas are without conceptual proliferation" precisely clarifies that dharmas transcend emotional attachments.
The four wisdoms are not real entities and are identical to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
since they are absent within true reality,
it is said that they do not exist.
If one says, "I shall see suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation,
and cultivate the path," this is mere conceptual proliferation and not the seeking of the Dharma.
This clarifies that sentient beings who grasp in such a manner are not truly seeking the Dharma.
This concludes the explanation of being free from a pure mind.
From the following line onward, it clarifies being free from the characteristics of purity:
"O Śāriputra, only the Dharma is called 'quiescence'."
This clarifies that phenomena are devoid of characteristics.

Within the established truths (*satya*), the arising and ceasing of the four truths is termed "not [quiescent]"; because this truth is free from these four characteristics, it is called "quiescent" (*śānta*).
If one practices seeking arising and ceasing, this is merely seeking arising and ceasing; this clarifies that those with minds characterized by signs are not truly seeking the Dharma.
Among the Four Noble Truths, the truth of cessation is unconditioned and is designated as "cessation."
To practice this arising and ceasing is not to seek [the Dharma]; if one perceives signs of purity within existence, that is not the true seeking of the Dharma.
From here below, there are eight phrases arranged in four pairs; regarding the true seeking of the Dharma, there are first four phrases arranged in two pairs.
This clarifies the method of transcending number.
Next, [it clarifies] transcending the mind-king.
Within the preceding method of transcending number, the first two lines constitute one pair.
The "clear" [refers to] the category of freedom from craving and the category of wisdom free from craving.
Within the state of freedom from craving, the former phrase lacks a mind capable of objective apprehension;
the latter phrase refers to that which is called "untainted" (*anāsakta*).
The mind that greedily clings to and names things is called "defilement" (rajas).
Within true reality, there is no such luminous dharma that transcends the realm of sentient beings.
If one becomes defiled by dharmas, even up to nirvāṇa itself.
This is attachment and not the seeking of the Dharma. If one is stained by the Dharma—
whether stained by the dharmas of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) or even stained by the dharmas of ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) such as nirvāṇa— it is not the seeking of the Dharma.
This clarifies that sentient beings who grasp are not truly seeking the Dharma.
The following phrase clarifies the object free from craving:
"The Dharma is without grasping or abandoning."
Regarding the objects of craving, that which is perceived as excellent should be grasped and that which is perceived as inferior must be abandoned;
within reality, one is free from these,
and thus there is neither grasping nor abandoning.
This clarifies that the dharma which is free from characteristics is called the dharma of taking and abandoning;
thus, such taking and abandoning is not the seeking of the dharma.
This clarifies that those whose minds possess characteristics are not truly seeking the dharma.
The following two lines clarify the separation from the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā*).
The preceding line clarifies the mind separated from wisdom,
while the subsequent line clarifies the objects of perception separated from wisdom.
Regarding "the Dharma has no place of practice":
because the mind of wisdom grasps the true center where there is no such thing, it has no place of practice.
This clarifies that the Dharma transcends emotional conceptualization.
If one practices such [erroneous] conduct, it is not the practice of seeking the Dharma.
This clarifies that the sentient being who grasps is not [the subject], and that the dharmas which are the objects of perception have no location.
Regarding the boundaries of the sphere... [omitted] ...the dharmas, within the state of suchness, are devoid of this location.
Therefore, it is said that... [omitted] ...the location.
This is an attachment; it is not the seeking of the Dharma.
This clarifies that those who possess a [discriminating] mind... [omitted]. These two pairs of phrases clarify the completion of the departure from numerical dharmas.
From here below, there are four phrases arranged in two pairs.
The first pair clarifies the detachment from the seven consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness, the sovereign minds (*citta-rāja*). In the latter pair of phrases:
The former phrase excludes the cognizing mind;
the latter phrase excludes the perceived object.
The term "dharma" refers to the *ālayavijñāna*.
To explain it according to the traditional interpretation,
this refers to the mark of a personal self (*pudgala-nimitta*).
According to contemporary new interpretations, it extends to the mark of a phenomenal self (*dharma-nimitta*).
The ālayavijñāna also permeates the characteristics of both the self of persons and the self of phenomena;
because it is free from these characteristics within the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā),
it is called "signless" (animitta).
This clarifies that when the Dharma transcends mental constructs, if one follows the consciousness of appearances,
then one is seeking appearances rather than seeking the Dharma.
This clarifies that sentient beings who grasp [at phenomena] are not truly seeking the Dharma.
The following line, "separated from the object of perception;
dharmas cannot abide," [indicates that] ... acts as consciousness.
That which is relied upon is called "abiding.
Since it is separated from this within true reality, it is said to be "impossible.
This clarifies that dharmas transcend characteristics.
If one dwells in dharmas,
this is dwelling in dharmas rather than seeking the Dharma.
This clarifies that those with a mind characterized by signs are not truly seeking the Dharma.
The following two lines form a pair clarifying the departure from the six consciousnesses, which are the mental kings (*cittarāja*).
The preceding line departs from the perceiving mind (*ālambaka-citta*),
while the succeeding line departs from the perceived objects (*ālambana-viṣaya*).
Regarding the Dharma that cannot be seen, heard, or cognized by wisdom:
it is seen when visual consciousness arises accordingly;
it is heard when auditory consciousness arises accordingly.
The three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body give rise to sensation accordingly,
while the mental consciousness gives rise to cognition accordingly.
Within the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmas*), the characteristics of these six consciousnesses are not at all [real entities] that emerge from sentient beings.
If one acts upon seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, this is merely seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; such a person is not truly seeking the Dharma.

The following sentence clarifies that when consciousness conditions objects, its four phases undergo transformation and change—this is termed [the cycle of birth and death]. For this reason, it is clarified here that the Dharma transcends these appearances.
If one practices the conditioned, this is seeking the conditioned and not seeking the Dharma; [therefore] it is not called seeking the Dharma.
The preceding section concludes the exposition of the teaching.
From here on, as for the passage beginning with "Therefore, Śāriputra, all dharmas should be sought with nothing to seek," [it means as follows]:
The conclusion summarizes the exhortation to practice.
Below, it further clarifies that through the [practice of] □□□□□□, one attains the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-vyavasthāna*).
At the initial stage, the eye of Dharma regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) becomes pure.
From here below is the third section, clarifying Vimalakīrti’s taking of his seat.
A question is asked:
Why did Vimalakīrti not simply take the seat himself, rather than first requiring instruction and reprimand?
The answer is:
The realm of the Buddhas, such as that of the Lamp-King (Dīpaṃkara), is inconceivable.

If one does not first reprove the mind that clings to attainment so as to cause it to abandon [such grasping], and instead causes [the practitioner] to practice the contemplation of non-attainment, thereby establishing the causal basis for their own portion of virtue, they will not be able to ascend the seat of the Lamp-King. For this reason, it is necessary to first provide instruction and reproof.
Regarding the section on taking the seat, there are five distinct parts:
first, Vimalakīrti asks Mañjuśrī about his seat;

second, Mañjuśrī’s statement beginning with "In the east" indicates the location of the seat; third, from "Then the elder manifested his supernatural powers" onwards, it clarifies how he took the high seat and entered the small room.
The fourth section, from "The various bodhisattvas and great disciples" onwards, clarifies the astonishment of the great assembly.
The fifth section, from "At that time, Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī" onwards, commands the assembly to be seated.
The textual characteristics are easy to perceive;
there is no need for detailed analysis. Question:
Vimalakīrti surely knows of the sublime seats throughout the ten directions;
why not simply take Mañjuśrī? He replied:
To clarify the inconceivable virtues based on reality—[omitted]—it refers to Vimalakīrti’s manifestation of a transformation body according to his proximity;
he now questions Mañjuśrī.
Because Mañjuśrī, being truly [powerful], can reach out from a very great distance to bring [the Dharma] here, we know that even those who are far away obtain benefit upon hearing this teaching.
Regarding the fifth [section], among the assembly of those summoned to sit, after [the mention of] Subhūti, he next summons the śrāvakas.
Among those summoned to sit as śrāvakas, Śāriputra and Subhūti were unable to sit.
Third, it instructs one in the ritual of prostrating to the Buddha; fourth, it clarifies the [benefits] of that prostration.
Subhūti, a Great Virtuous Arhat endowed with supernormal powers—why was he unable to sit [in meditation]? This was merely sitting for worldly matters.
Śāriputra was not merely able to sit [there].
This is truly because this seat was accomplished through the power of the vows of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara;
it is not within the realm of the supernatural powers of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Therefore, he was unable to sit.
Only through the power of the Buddha’s spiritual authority (*ṛddhi*) and the observance of propriety did he finally manage to take his seat.
Thus concludes the account of how Vimalakīrti, in response to Śāriputra’s thought regarding the seating arrangement, [performed] the aforementioned [miracle].

From here below is the second section, which, based on the person Śāriputra, praises Vimalakīrti’s oral proclamation of inconceivable matters. [Regarding this,] the commentary provides a structural analysis.
Someone raises an objection, saying:
"A mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru":
since this is already inconceivable, the mustard seed itself is also inconceivable.
It is not answered by saying "Mount Sumeru contains the mustard seed," nor is it said that "the mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru."
To attain this is inconceivable.
Just as Mount Sumeru can be contained [within a mustard seed], so too can one eon be shortened to seven days. Is this not inconceivable? He replied:
Distinguishing phenomena through debate involves receiving the guest by means of the small to receive the great;
it is not that the phenomena themselves are extended or shortened.
Therefore, regarding the brief summary and the corresponding details:
it is like a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru.
